doc.title: Winard Harper interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, October 10, 2014

title: Lessons from Betty Carter: strength, business sense and boot camp
summary: Harper admired Carter's tenacity, how she created her own concerts, and her tough band as a boot camp.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: A lot of everything. A lot of music, but partly more life than anything. Because one thing about Betty that I always admired was her strength, and she was tenacious. She was going to find a way to get it done. And we miss that. And I think the music misses that, those kind of people like that. Betty, you know, she would think — if a door was closed she used to go open up something somewhere else. Because I remember many times just asking her questions all the time. And she had ways of, okay well if this club is not going to hire me well I don’t like that club and I’m going to do this, we’ll go in here, we’ll play this city but we’ll play here. You know sometimes too she would rent out a theater or space and she put herself in concert. So I really admired that and it helped me a lot when I started the Harper Brothers. So business-wise I learned a lot of from Betty and her strength, and just how to keep a band and how to try to get what you want from everybody. Keep everybody on the same page and playing the music.
Was she tough with her accompanists?

Sure. But it was — I always looked at it like a boot camp. You know what I mean? You know if you come in there and you get through this then you’re ready for any- and everything. And then when I looked at the history of it, come to find out a lot of the guys that played with her, when they came out into the scene, when they got from beyond her, they were — they could handle just about anything you threw at them. And I think a lot of the other guys around knew that. Well this guy played with Betty so I know he’s going to be sound, he’s going to know a lot of tunes. So those things came with the territory. So I kind of felt like if you can get through that, you know, you can make it and you can do it well and you’ve graduated. So she was tough but in a good way as long as you looked at it the right way. You know, you had to see the light at the end of the tunnel.
